meta.titre: Deregulation Policy: opening markets to competition and its limits

sections.contenu_markdown: Suppose a city allows only one licensed company to run minibuses on a busy route in Douala. Fares are high and the service is infrequent. The government then removes the licence limit and many operators enter. This is deregulation. It appears in examinations as a supply-side policy that is easy to confuse with privatisation, so you must define it precisely and weigh its benefits against its risks.

items: A monopoly is a market with a single seller.
Competition tends to lower prices and improve quality.
Supply-side policies aim to increase the productive capacity of the economy.
Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Definition
**Deregulation** is the removal or relaxation of government rules that restrict how firms operate, especially rules that limit **entry into and exit from a market** and the amount of **competition**. Examples: ending a legal monopoly, scrapping a licence that limits the number of firms, removing price controls. It is a **supply-side policy**: it aims to raise efficiency and output by making markets more competitive.

Do not confuse it with other policies:

| Policy | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Deregulation | Removing rules that restrict entry, exit or competition; ownership does not change |
| Privatisation | Transferring ownership of a state firm to private owners |
| Nationalisation | Government takes over a private firm |
| Subsidy | Payment to producers to lower their costs |

### Why it may work
More firms can enter, so prices tend to fall and quality, choice and innovation tend to rise. Firms must cut costs to survive, which improves productive efficiency and reduces **X-inefficiency** (the waste that arises when a firm faces little competition). Lower barriers also help new small firms and reduce government administration costs. By lowering costs and raising output, it can shift long-run aggregate supply to the right.

### Why it may fail
| Problem | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Market power remains | A few firms may dominate and keep prices high |
| Natural monopolies | Where one firm can supply at lowest average cost (for example a water network), more firms may raise costs |
| Quality and safety | Firms may cut standards to cut costs |
| Externalities | Firms may ignore pollution or other costs to society |
| Losers | Job losses in protected firms; services to remote or poor areas may be dropped |
| Financial risk | Weaker control of banks may encourage excessive risk-taking |

### Evaluation
Results depend on the market structure, the strength of the remaining regulators, how elastic demand is, and the time allowed: gains take time, while job losses are immediate. Rarely is complete deregulation best; most economists favour removing barriers to competition while keeping rules on safety, pollution and natural monopolies.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use for definition or multiple-choice questions.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If the rule on entry, exit or competition is removed, it is deregulation. If ownership moves from the state to private investors, it is privatisation. If the government buys or seizes a private firm, it is nationalisation.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use for discuss, assess or to-what-extent questions.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Plan: (1) competition and prices, (2) efficiency and innovation, (3) risks (market power, quality, externalities, jobs), (4) judgement that depends on the market (natural monopoly or not) and on the regulator. Include one worked number if data are given.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when prices and quantities before and after are given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Percentage change in price and in quantity; elasticity $= \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P}$; change in expenditure $=$ new $P \times Q$ minus old $P \times Q$. State FCFA.

sections.enonce_markdown: A single licensed company runs buses on one route in a hypothetical city, charging 1,000 FCFA per trip for 20,000 trips a week. The government ends the licence limit. New operators enter, the price falls to 800 FCFA and trips rise to 28,000 a week. Discuss to what extent deregulating the route benefits consumers.

etapes.justification: "Discuss to what extent" requires both sides and a reasoned judgement, not a list of benefits.
Competition is the main mechanism, so use the given numbers. Price falls from 1,000 to 800 FCFA, a fall of 20%; trips rise from 20,000 to 28,000 per week, a rise of 40%.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Elasticity $= \frac{+40\%}{-20\%} = -2$ (elastic): lower prices raise total spending from 20,000,000 to 22,400,000 FCFA

etapes.justification: More firms mean more choice and pressure to cut costs.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Lower prices, higher quality and more frequent service are likely; operators must cut costs to survive.

etapes.justification: A balanced answer must show where deregulation can fail.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Safety standards may fall; rural routes may be dropped; one large firm may later dominate; job losses at the old operator.

etapes.justification: The judgement must depend on conditions.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Gains are large where entry is easy and demand is elastic; the risks are reduced by keeping safety rules and monitoring dominant firms.

etapes.justification: End with a direct answer to the question.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Deregulation benefits consumers to a large extent, provided that safety and competition are monitored.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer (key points).** Deregulation lowered the price by 20% and raised trips by 40%, which implies elastic demand (elasticity of -2), so total spending rose from 20,000,000 to 22,400,000 FCFA a week while each trip costs less. Competition also improves choice and pushes operators to cut costs. The risks are lower safety standards, loss of unprofitable rural routes, a later dominant firm and job losses at the old operator. Consumers benefit to a large extent if safety rules and competition are monitored.

items.erreur_markdown: "Deregulation is the sale of state firms to private owners."
items.pourquoi_faux: That is privatisation, where ownership changes. Deregulation removes rules and can happen without any change of ownership.
items.correction_markdown: Define deregulation as removing restrictions on entry, exit or competition.

items.pourquoi_faux: If market power remains, or if the market is a natural monopoly, prices may not fall and may even rise.
items.correction_markdown: Say that it **tends** to lower prices where competition really develops.

items.erreur_markdown: Listing advantages only in a "to what extent" question.
items.pourquoi_faux: The command word asks for a judgement, which needs both sides and a conclusion.
items.correction_markdown: Give benefits, risks, then a conclusion that depends on market conditions.

items.pourquoi_faux: It removes rules that restrict competition. Rules on safety, pollution and standards usually remain.
items.correction_markdown: Separate economic regulation (entry, prices) from social regulation (safety, environment).

items.erreur_markdown: Calculating elasticity as the change in quantity divided by the change in price in raw units.
items.pourquoi_faux: Elasticity uses percentage changes, so units cancel and the result is comparable across goods.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the policy in each case: (i) the government sells 60% of the shares of a state telecommunications firm to private investors; (ii) the government removes the licence requirement that limits the number of taxi firms in a city; (iii) the government takes control of a private water company.
items.solution_markdown: (i) **Privatisation** (ownership moves to private investors). (ii) **Deregulation** (a rule restricting entry is removed). (iii) **Nationalisation** (the government takes over a private firm).

items.enonce_markdown: After a market for mobile data bundles is opened to new firms, the price of a bundle falls from 2,000 to 1,600 FCFA and the quantity bought rises from 50,000 to 65,000 bundles per month. Calculate (a) the percentage changes in price and quantity, (b) the price elasticity of demand, (c) total consumer spending before and after, and (d) what consumers would have paid for 65,000 bundles at the old price, compared with the new spending.
Discuss to what extent deregulating the supply of piped water in a city would benefit consumers.
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for: possible benefits (competition between suppliers, lower prices, better service, investment by entrants); the natural monopoly problem (a pipe network is very costly to duplicate, so competing networks may raise average costs and one supplier may dominate anyway); quality and safety (water standards matter for health, so regulation of standards is still needed); fairness (poor or remote areas may be left unserved if firms serve only profitable customers); evaluation (outcomes depend on the strength of the regulator and on whether competition can be introduced in parts of the market, for example in billing or in supply to large users, while the network stays regulated); a reasoned judgement that consumers benefit only if the network monopoly is regulated and standards are enforced.

items_markdown: Deregulation removes rules that restrict entry, exit or competition; ownership does not change.
It is a supply-side policy: it can lower prices, raise efficiency and encourage innovation.
It differs from privatisation (change of ownership) and nationalisation (state takeover).
Risks: continuing market power, natural monopolies, lower standards, externalities, job losses and neglected areas.
Evaluate by market structure, strength of the regulator, elasticity and time; end with a reasoned judgement.
